description: Apollo landing sites and NASA's Artemis III candidate regions. Latitude/longitude in degrees, planetocentric, east-positive (west is negative). Artemis coordinates are approximate region centres. Apollo sites are near the equator and fall outside the 80°S polar map; they are kept here for the equatorial views.

sites.name: Apollo 11
sites.goal: Land the first humans on the Moon
facts: Neil Armstrong, Buzz Aldrin (surface) · Michael Collins (orbit)
≈ 21 h 36 min · 1 moonwalk of ≈ 2 h 31 min
sites.story: First crewed landing on the Moon. Armstrong had to fly the lunar module Eagle by hand to avoid a boulder field, with very little fuel left. Armstrong and then Aldrin walked on the surface, planted the US flag and set up a seismometer and a laser retroreflector that is still in use today. Splashdown on 24 July 1969.

sites.name: Apollo 12
sites.site: Oceanus Procellarum — next to the Surveyor 3 probe
sites.goal: Recover parts of the Surveyor 3 probe
facts: Pete Conrad, Alan Bean (surface) · Richard Gordon (orbit)
sites.story: The rocket was struck by lightning twice shortly after liftoff, but the mission continued. First precision landing: the crew touched down about 180 m from Surveyor 3 and brought back parts of it to study how the lunar environment had affected them. The astronauts also deployed the first complete ALSEP science station. Splashdown on 24 November 1969.

sites.name: Apollo 14
sites.goal: Study the ground of the Fra Mauro formation
facts: Alan Shepard, Edgar Mitchell (surface) · Stuart Roosa (orbit)
sites.story: Apollo 14 went to Fra Mauro, the target Apollo 13 never reached, to sample material thought to be ejecta from the Imbrium basin. The crew pulled their tools and samples on a hand cart, and Shepard famously hit two golf balls on the surface. Splashdown on 9 February 1971.

sites.name: Apollo 15
sites.site: Hadley–Apennine — at the foot of the Apennines, near Hadley Rille
sites.goal: Study a geologically interesting region with a valley and lunar mountains
facts: David Scott, James Irwin (surface) · Alfred Worden (orbit)
sites.story: First 'J' mission: longer and more scientific, with the first Lunar Roving Vehicle, which covered about 28 km. The crew brought back the 'Genesis Rock', a piece of very old lunar crust. Scott also dropped a hammer and a feather on camera to show that they fall at the same rate without air. Splashdown on 7 August 1971.

sites.name: Apollo 16
sites.goal: Sample the lunar highlands, thought to be volcanic at Descartes
facts: John Young, Charles Duke (surface) · Ken Mattingly (orbit)
sites.story: The only Apollo landing in the central highlands. Geologists expected volcanic rocks, but the samples were mostly impact breccias, which changed how the highlands were understood. The crew drove the lunar rover about 27 km. Splashdown on 27 April 1972.

sites.name: Apollo 17
sites.site: Taurus–Littrow — a valley bordered by mountain massifs
sites.goal: Sample old highland rock and young volcanic material in one valley
facts: Eugene Cernan, Harrison Schmitt (surface) · Ronald Evans (orbit)
sites.story: The last crewed mission to the Moon to date. Harrison Schmitt, the only geologist to walk on the Moon, found orange soil made of volcanic glass beads more than 3 billion years old. The crew drove about 36 km in the rover. The famous 'Blue Marble' photo of Earth was taken on the way out. Splashdown on 19 December 1972.

sites.name: Peak near Cabeus B
sites.site: Artemis III candidate region — a peak near the crater Cabeus B
sites.goal: Crewed landing near permanently shadowed regions
sites.story: One of the nine candidate landing regions NASA identified for Artemis III. It sits near Cabeus, the crater where the LCROSS impactor detected water ice in 2009.

sites.name: Haworth
sites.site: Artemis III candidate region — by Haworth crater
sites.goal: Crewed landing near permanently shadowed regions
sites.story: One of the nine candidate landing regions NASA identified for Artemis III, next to Haworth, a large permanently shadowed crater and one of the coldest places on the map.

sites.name: Malapert Massif
sites.site: Artemis III candidate region — Malapert Massif
sites.goal: Crewed landing near permanently shadowed regions
sites.story: One of the nine candidate landing regions NASA identified for Artemis III. Malapert is a large mountain massif on the Earth-facing side of the pole, which helps direct communication with Earth.
